paragraphs: The practical consequences of these different systems are easy to see. A careful observer will soon notice that the business of the Union is far better conducted than that of any individual State. The Federal government acts more fairly and more moderately than the States do. Its designs show more wisdom, its projects are more lasting and more skillfully combined, and its measures are carried out with more vigor and consistency.

I will sum up the substance of this chapter in a few words. The existence of democracies is threatened by two dangers: the complete subjection of the legislative body to the whims of the electoral body, and the concentration of all the powers of government in the legislative authority. The legislators of the States have encouraged the growth of these evils. The legislators of the Union have resisted them by every means within their control.

Characteristics That Distinguish the Federal Constitution of the United States of America from All Other Federal Constitutions — The American Union seems to resemble all other confederations — Nevertheless its effects are different — The reason for this — How the Union differs from all other confederations — The American government is not a federal government but an imperfect national government.

The United States of America is neither the first nor the only example of confederate States. Several have existed in modern Europe, not to mention those of antiquity. Switzerland, the Germanic Empire, and the Republic of the United Provinces either were or still are confederations. When the student of politics examines the constitutions of these countries, he is surprised to find that the powers they gave the Federal government are nearly identical to those the American Constitution gives the government of the United States. They give the central power the same rights of making peace and war, of raising money and troops, and of providing for the general needs and common interests of the nation. Nevertheless, the Federal government of these other peoples has always been as remarkable for its weakness and inefficiency as that of the Union is for its vigor and enterprise. Again, the first American Confederation perished because its government was too weak, and yet that weak government held rights even more extensive than those of the Federal government today. But the more recent Constitution of the United States contains certain principles that have a most important influence, although they do not strike the observer at once.

This Constitution may at first sight be confused with the federal constitutions that came before it, but it rests on a new theory, which may be considered a great invention in modern political science. In all the confederations formed before the American Constitution of 1789, the allied States agreed to obey the directions of a Federal government, but they kept for themselves the right to order and enforce the execution of the laws of the Union. The American States that joined together in 1789 agreed that the Federal government should not only make the laws but also carry out its own enactments. In both cases the right is the same, but the way it is exercised is different, and this difference produced the most momentous consequences.

In all the confederations formed before the American Union, the Federal government demanded its supplies from the separate governments. If the measure it prescribed was burdensome to any one of those bodies, ways were found to evade its claims. A powerful State resorted to arms; a weak one tolerated the resistance that the law of the Union, its sovereign, met with, and fell back on inaction under the excuse of inability. In these circumstances one of two outcomes has invariably occurred. Either the most dominant of the allied peoples has taken over the privileges of the Federal authority and ruled all the States in its name, *p or the Federal government has been abandoned by its natural supporters, anarchy has arisen among the confederates, and the Union has lost all power to act. *q

p [ This was the case in Greece, when Philip undertook to execute the decree of the Amphictyons; in the Low Countries, where the province of Holland always gave the law; and, in our own time, in the Germanic Confederation, in which Austria and Prussia assume a great degree of influence over the whole country, in the name of the Diet.]
q [ Such has always been the situation of the Swiss Confederation, which would have perished ages ago but for the mutual jealousies of its neighbors.]

In America the subjects of the Union are not States but private citizens. The national government levies a tax not on the State of Massachusetts but on each inhabitant of Massachusetts. All earlier confederate governments presided over communities, but the government of the Union rules individuals. Its force is not borrowed but its own, and it is served by its own civil and military officers, its own army, and its own courts of justice. There is no doubt that the spirit of the nation, the passions of the multitude, and the local prejudices of each State tend strongly to weaken the authority of a Federal power constituted in this way, and to make it easier to resist its commands. But the comparative weakness of a limited sovereignty is an evil inherent in the federal system. In America, each State has fewer opportunities to resist and fewer temptations to refuse compliance. Nor can such a plan be carried out (if it is entertained at all) without an open violation of the laws of the Union, a direct interruption of the ordinary course of justice, and a bold declaration of revolt — in a word, without taking a decisive step that men hesitate to take.

In all earlier confederations, the privileges of the Union furnished more causes of discord than of power, since they multiplied the claims of the nation without increasing the means of enforcing them. Accordingly, we may note that the real weakness of federal governments has almost always been in exact proportion to their nominal power. This is not the case in the American Union, where, as in ordinary governments, the Federal government has the means of enforcing everything it is empowered to demand.

The human mind invents new things more easily than new words, and so we are forced to use a multitude of improper and inadequate expressions. When several nations form a permanent league and establish a supreme authority, which does not have the same influence over the members of the community as a national government but acts on each of the Confederate States as a whole, this government, so essentially different from all others, is called a Federal one. Later another form of society is discovered, in which several peoples are fused into one and the same nation with regard to certain common interests, while they remain distinct, or at least only confederate, with regard to all their other concerns. In this case the central power acts directly on those it governs, rules, and judges, in the same manner as a national government but within a more limited sphere. Here the term Federal government clearly no longer applies to a state of things that must be called an incomplete national government. A form of government has been found that is neither exactly national nor federal. But no further progress has been made, and the new word that will one day name this new invention does not yet exist.

The lack of this new kind of confederation has brought all earlier Unions to civil war, to subjection, or to a stagnant apathy. The peoples that formed these leagues were either too dull to see this great remedy or too timid to apply it. The American Confederation perished from the same defects.

But the Confederate States of America had long been accustomed to forming part of one empire before they won their independence. They had not acquired the habit of governing themselves, and their national prejudices had not taken deep root in their minds. Superior to the rest of the world in political knowledge, and sharing that knowledge equally among themselves, they were little troubled by the passions that generally oppose the extension of federal authority in a nation, and the wisdom of the leading citizens kept those passions in check. The Americans applied the remedy with prudent firmness as soon as they became aware of the evil. They amended their laws, and they saved their country.
Advantages of the Federal System in General, and Its Special Usefulness in America.

Happiness and freedom of small nations — Power of great nations — Great empires favorable to the growth of civilization — Strength is often the first element of national prosperity — The aim of the Federal system is to unite the twofold advantages of a small and a large territory — Advantages the United States has gained from this system — The law adapts itself to the needs of the population; the population does not conform to the needs of the law — Activity, improvement, and love and enjoyment of freedom in the American communities — The public spirit of the Union is the summary of provincial patriotism — Principles and things circulate freely over the territory of the United States — The Union is happy and free like a small nation, and respected like a great empire.

In small nations the scrutiny of society reaches into every part, and the spirit of improvement enters into the smallest details. The ambition of the people is necessarily held in check by its weakness, so all the efforts and resources of the citizens are turned to the internal benefit of the community and are not likely to vanish in the fleeting breath of glory. The desires of every individual are limited, because extraordinary abilities are rarely found. The gifts of an equal fortune make the various conditions of life uniform, and the customs of the inhabitants are orderly and simple. So if we weigh the degrees of popular morality and education, we shall generally find that small nations have more people in easy circumstances, a more numerous population, and a more tranquil society than great empires do.

When tyranny is established in the heart of a small nation, it is more galling than elsewhere. Because it acts within a narrow circle, every point of that circle is subject to its direct influence. It makes up for the great designs it cannot entertain by violent or exasperating interference in a multitude of minute details. It leaves the political world, to which it properly belongs, to meddle with the arrangements of domestic life. Tastes as well as actions are to be regulated at its pleasure, and the families of the citizens as well as the affairs of the State are to be governed by its decisions. This invasion of rights, however, occurs only rarely, and freedom is in truth the natural state of small communities. The temptations that government offers to ambition are too weak, and the resources of private individuals are too slight, for the sovereign power easily to fall into the grasp of a single citizen. And if such a thing did happen, the subjects of the State could without difficulty overthrow the tyrant and his oppression by a simultaneous effort.

Small nations have therefore always been the birthplace of political liberty. Many of them have lost their freedoms by expanding their dominion, and this shows that the freedom they enjoyed owed more to their small size than to the character of their people.

No great nation in the history of the world has kept a republican form of government for a long series of years, *r and this has led people to conclude that such a thing is impracticable. For my part, I cannot help blaming the imprudence of a being who tries to limit the possible and to judge the future. He is deceived every hour by the most obvious realities of life, and he is constantly taken by surprise in the circumstances he knows best. But it may be said with confidence that a great republic will always be exposed to far greater perils than a small one.
r [ I do not speak of a confederation of small republics, but of a great consolidated Republic.]

All the passions most fatal to republican institutions spread as territory grows, while the virtues that maintain their dignity do not grow in the same proportion. The ambition of the citizens increases with the power of the State, and the strength of parties with the importance of the ends they have in view. But devotion to the common good, which is the surest check on destructive passions, is no stronger in a large republic than in a small one. Indeed, it could easily be proved that it is weaker and less sincere. The arrogance of wealth and the dejection of the wretched, capital cities of unusual size, a lax morality, a vulgar selfishness, and a great confusion of interests — these are the dangers that almost invariably arise from the great size of States. But several of these evils are hardly harmful to a monarchy, and some of them help to maintain it. In monarchical States the strength of the government is its own; it may use the community, but it does not depend on it, and the authority of the prince is proportioned to the prosperity of the nation. But the only security a republican government has against these evils lies in the support of the majority. This support is not proportionally greater in a large republic than in a small one. So while the means of attack constantly increase in both number and influence, the power of resistance remains the same, or rather it may be said to diminish, since the inclinations and interests of the people become more varied as the population grows, and the difficulty of forming a solid majority keeps increasing. It has also been observed that the intensity of human passions is heightened not only by the importance of the end they aim at but by the number of individuals who are moved by them at the same time. Everyone has had occasion to notice that his emotions in the midst of a sympathetic crowd are far greater than those he would have felt alone. In great republics the force of political passion is irresistible, not only because it aims at gigantic purposes, but because it is felt and shared by millions of men at the same time.

It may therefore be stated as a general proposition that nothing is more opposed to the well-being and the freedom of man than vast empires. Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge the particular advantages of great States. The very reason that makes the desire for power more intense in these communities than among ordinary men also makes the love of glory more prominent in the hearts of one class of citizens, who regard the applause of a great people as a reward worthy of their efforts and as an uplifting encouragement. If we want to learn why great nations contribute more powerfully to the spread of human improvement than small States do, we shall find an adequate cause in the rapid and energetic circulation of ideas, and in those great cities that are the intellectual centers where all the rays of human genius are reflected and combined. To this it may be added that most important discoveries require a display of national power that the government of a small State cannot make. In great nations the government entertains a greater number of general ideas, and it is more completely free from the routine of precedent and the selfishness of local prejudice. Its designs are conceived with more talent and carried out with more boldness.

In time of peace the well-being of small nations is undoubtedly more general and more complete. But they tend to suffer more acutely from the calamities of war than great empires do. The distant frontiers of great empires may for ages keep danger away from the mass of the people, who are therefore more often afflicted than ruined by war.

But in this matter, as in many others, the argument from necessity outweighs all others. If only small nations existed, I do not doubt that mankind would be happier and freer, but the existence of great nations is unavoidable.

This consideration introduces physical strength as a condition of national prosperity. It profits a people little to be wealthy and free if it is perpetually exposed to being plundered or conquered. The number of its manufactures and the extent of its commerce are of little advantage if another nation commands the seas and gives the law in all the markets of the globe. Small nations are often poor not because they are small but because they are weak, and great empires prosper less because they are great than because they are strong. Physical strength is therefore one of the first conditions of the happiness, and even of the existence, of nations. Hence it happens that, unless very unusual circumstances intervene, small nations are always joined to large empires in the end, either by force or by their own consent. Yet I know of no more deplorable spectacle than that of a people unable either to defend or to maintain its independence.

The Federal system was created with the intention of combining the different advantages of larger and smaller nations, and a single glance at the United States of America is enough to see the advantages they have drawn from adopting it.

In great centralized nations the legislator is obliged to give the laws a uniform character that does not always suit the variety of customs and districts. Since he takes no notice of particular cases, he can only proceed on general principles. The population is obliged to conform to the demands of the legislation, because the legislation cannot adapt itself to the needs and customs of the population, and this is the cause of endless trouble and misery. This disadvantage does not exist in confederations. Congress regulates the principal measures of the national government, and all the details of administration are left to the provincial legislatures. It is impossible to imagine how much this division of sovereignty contributes to the well-being of each of the States that make up the Union. These small communities are never troubled by the desire for expansion or the cares of self-defense, so all public authority and private energy is employed in internal improvement. The central government of each State, being in immediate contact with the citizens, is informed daily of the needs that arise in society. New projects are proposed every year, discussed either at town meetings or by the legislature of the State, and passed on by the press to stimulate the zeal and excite the interest of the citizens. This spirit of improvement is constantly alive in the American republics without disturbing their tranquillity. The ambition for power gives way to the less refined and less dangerous love of comfort. It is generally believed in America that the existence and permanence of the republican form of government in the New World depend on the existence and permanence of the Federal system. It is not unusual to blame a large share of the misfortunes of the new States of South America on the unwise creation of great republics instead of a divided and confederate sovereignty.

It is beyond dispute that the love and the habits of republican government in the United States were produced in the townships and in the provincial assemblies. In a small State like Connecticut, for instance, cutting a canal or building a road is a weighty political question. The State has no army to pay and no wars to wage, and it cannot bestow much wealth or honor on its leading citizens. In such a State no form of government could be more natural or more suitable than a republic. But it is this same republican spirit, these manners and customs of a free people, produced and nurtured in the different States, that are afterward applied to the country at large. The public spirit of the Union is, so to speak, nothing more than a summary of the patriotic zeal of the provinces. Every citizen of the United States transfers his attachment to his little republic into the common store of American patriotism. In defending the Union he defends the growing prosperity of his own district, the right to conduct its affairs, and the hope of getting improvements adopted that may favor his own interest. These are motives that move men more readily than the general interests of the country and the glory of the nation.

On the other hand, if the temper and the customs of the inhabitants especially fitted them to promote the welfare of a great republic, the Federal system cleared away the obstacles they might have met. The confederation of all the American States has none of the ordinary disadvantages that result from great concentrations of people. The Union is a great republic in size, but the small number of objects its government provides for makes it resemble a small State. Its acts are important, but they are rare. Because the sovereignty of the Union is limited and incomplete, its exercise is not incompatible with liberty, for it does not excite those insatiable desires for fame and power that have proved so fatal to great republics. Because the country has no common center, vast capital cities, colossal wealth, abject poverty, and sudden revolutions are all unknown. Political passion, instead of sweeping over the land like a torrent of desolation, spends its strength against the interests and individual passions of each State.

Nevertheless, all goods and ideas circulate throughout the Union as freely as in a country inhabited by one people. Nothing checks the spirit of enterprise. The government makes use of the help of everyone who has talents or knowledge to serve it. Within the frontiers of the Union the profoundest peace prevails, as in the heart of some great empire. Abroad, the Union ranks with the most powerful nations of the earth. Two thousand miles of coast are open to the commerce of the world, and because it holds the keys of the globe, its flag is respected in the most distant seas. The Union is as happy and as free as a small people, and as glorious and as strong as a great nation.
Why the Federal System Is Not Suited to All Peoples, and How the Anglo-Americans Were Able to Adopt It.

Every Federal system contains defects that baffle the efforts of the legislator — The Federal system is complex — It demands a daily exercise of judgment on the part of the citizens — Practical knowledge of government is common among the Americans — The relative weakness of the government of the Union, another defect inherent in the Federal system — The Americans have reduced it without remedying it — The sovereignty of the separate States appears weaker, but is really stronger, than that of the Union — Why? — Natural causes of union must exist between confederate peoples besides the laws — What these causes are among the Anglo-Americans — Maine and Georgia, separated by a distance of a thousand miles, are more naturally united than Normandy and Brittany — War, the main danger of confederations — This is proved even by the example of the United States — The Union has no great wars to fear — Why? — Dangers to which Europeans would be exposed if they adopted the Federal system of the Americans.

When a legislator succeeds, after persistent efforts, in exerting an indirect influence on the destiny of nations, mankind praises his genius. But in fact the geographical position of the country, which he cannot change, a social condition that arose without his help, customs and opinions whose source he cannot trace, and an origin he does not know all exercise such an irresistible influence over the course of society that he himself is carried away by the current after a futile resistance. Like the navigator, he may steer the vessel that carries him along, but he can neither change its structure, nor raise the winds, nor calm the waters that swell beneath him.

I have shown the advantages the Americans draw from their federal system. It remains for me to point out the circumstances that made that system workable, since not all nations can enjoy its benefits. The incidental defects of the Federal system that come from the laws may be corrected by the skill of the legislator. But there are further evils inherent in the system that the peoples who adopt it cannot counteract. These nations must therefore find the strength needed to bear the natural imperfections of their government.

The most prominent evil of all Federal systems is the very complex nature of the means they employ. Two sovereignties necessarily stand face to face. The legislator may simplify and balance the action of these two sovereignties by limiting each to a carefully defined sphere of authority. But he cannot merge them into one, or prevent them from coming into collision at certain points. The Federal system therefore rests on a theory that is necessarily complicated, and that requires those it governs to exercise a considerable amount of judgment every day.

A proposition must be plain to be accepted by the understanding of a people. A false idea that is clear and precise will always win more followers in the world than a true principle that is obscure or involved. Hence parties, which are like small communities within the nation, invariably adopt some principle or some name as a symbol. This symbol represents very inadequately the end they have in view and the means at their disposal, but without it they could neither act nor survive. Governments founded on a single principle or a single feeling that is easily defined are perhaps not the best, but they are unquestionably the strongest and the most lasting in the world.

On the other hand, when one examines the Constitution of the United States, the most perfect federal constitution that ever existed, one is startled by the variety of knowledge and the excellence of judgment that it presupposes in the people it is meant to govern. The government of the Union depends entirely on legal fictions. The Union is an ideal nation that exists only in the mind, and its limits and extent can be discerned only by the understanding.

Once the general theory is understood, countless difficulties remain to be solved in applying it. The sovereignty of the Union is so entangled with that of the States that it is impossible to see its boundaries at first glance. The whole structure of the government is artificial and conventional. It would be poorly suited to a people that has not long been accustomed to conducting its own affairs, or to one in which the science of politics has not reached the humblest classes of society. I have never been more struck by the good sense and practical judgment of the Americans than in the ingenious devices by which they get around the countless difficulties arising from their Federal Constitution. I have scarcely ever met a plain American citizen who could not distinguish, with surprising ease, the obligations created by the laws of Congress from those created by the laws of his own State, or who, after separating the matters that fall under the authority of the Union from those the local legislature is competent to regulate, could not point out the exact limits of the several jurisdictions of the Federal courts and the tribunals of the State.

The Constitution of the United States is like those exquisite products of human skill that bring wealth and renown to their inventors but are worthless in any other hands. This truth is shown by the condition of Mexico at the present time. The Mexicans wanted to establish a federal system. They took the Federal Constitution of their neighbors, the Anglo-Americans, as their model and copied it with considerable accuracy. *s But although they had borrowed the letter of the law, they were unable to create or introduce the spirit and meaning that give it life. They were caught in ceaseless difficulties between the machinery of their double government. The sovereignty of the States and that of the Union perpetually exceeded their respective privileges and came into collision. To this day Mexico is alternately the victim of anarchy and the slave of military despotism.
s [ See the Mexican Constitution of 1824.]

The second and most fatal of all the defects I have mentioned, and the one I believe to be inherent in the federal system, is the relative weakness of the government of the Union. The principle on which all confederations rest is that of a divided sovereignty. The legislator may make this division less noticeable, and he may even hide it for a time from the public eye, but he cannot prevent it from existing, and a divided sovereignty must always be less powerful than a complete supremacy. The reader has seen, from my remarks on the Constitution of the United States, that the Americans have shown unusual ingenuity in combining two things. One is the restriction of the power of the Union within the narrow limits of a federal government. The other is the appearance, and to a certain extent the force, of a national government. By this means the legislators of the Union have succeeded in reducing, though not in neutralizing, the natural danger of confederations.

It has been observed that the American government does not address itself to the States but sends its commands directly to the citizens, and compels them as isolated individuals to comply with its demands. But suppose a Federal law clashed with the interests and prejudices of a State. It might be feared that all the citizens of that State would consider themselves interested in the cause of a single individual who refused to obey. Suppose all the citizens of the State were aggrieved at the same time and in the same way by the authority of the Union. The Federal government would try in vain to subdue them one by one. They would instinctively unite in a common defense, and they would draw a ready-made organization from the share of sovereignty that the institutions of their State allow them to enjoy. Fiction would give way to reality, and an organized portion of the territory might then contest the central authority. *t The same observation holds true of the Federal jurisdiction. Suppose the courts of the Union violated an important law of a State in a private case. The real contest, if not the apparent one, would then arise between the aggrieved State, represented by a citizen, and the Union, represented by its courts of justice. *u

t [ [This is precisely what occurred in 1862, and the following paragraph describes correctly the feelings and ideas of the South. General Lee held that his primary allegiance was due, not to the Union, but to Virginia.]]

u [ For instance, the Union has the right under the Constitution to sell unoccupied lands for its own profit. Suppose the State of Ohio claimed the same right for certain territories within its boundaries, on the grounds that the Constitution refers only to lands that do not belong to the jurisdiction of any particular State, and so chose to dispose of them itself. The lawsuit would be carried on in the names of the purchasers from the State of Ohio and the purchasers from the Union, and not in the names of Ohio and the Union. But what would become of this legal fiction if the Federal purchaser was confirmed in his right by the courts of the Union, while the other claimant was ordered to keep possession by the tribunals of the State of Ohio?]

He would have only a partial knowledge of the world who imagined that legal fictions can stop men from finding and using the means of gratifying their passions that have been left open to them. It may be doubted whether the American legislators, in making a collision between the two sovereigns less probable, removed the cause of such a misfortune. It may even be said that they were unable to ensure that the Federal element would prevail in a case of this kind. The Union has money and troops, but the affections and prejudices of the people lie with the States. The sovereignty of the Union is an abstract being, connected with few external objects. The sovereignty of the States is perceptible every hour, easily understood, and constantly active. And if the former is of recent creation, the latter is as old as the people itself. The sovereignty of the Union is artificial; that of the States is natural, and it draws its existence from its own simple influence, like the authority of a parent. The supreme power of the nation affects only a few of the chief interests of society. It represents an immense but remote country, and it claims a feeling of patriotism that is vague and ill defined. But the authority of the States controls every individual citizen at every hour and in all circumstances. It protects his property, his freedom, and his life. When we recall the traditions, the customs, and the prejudices of local and familiar attachment with which it is bound up, we cannot doubt the superiority of a power that is interwoven with every circumstance that makes love of one’s native country instinctive in the human heart.

Legislators cannot prevent the dangerous collisions that occur between the two sovereignties coexisting in the federal system. Their first object must therefore be, not only to dissuade the confederate States from warfare, but also to encourage institutions that may help maintain peace. It follows that the Federal compact cannot last unless the communities leagued together have a certain number of inducements to union that make their common dependence agreeable and the task of the government light. And that system cannot succeed without favorable circumstances in addition to the influence of good laws. All the peoples that have ever formed a confederation have been held together by a certain number of common interests, which served as the intellectual ties of association.

But the feelings and principles of man must be taken into account as well as his immediate interests. A certain uniformity of civilization is no less necessary to the durability of a confederation than a uniformity of interests among the States that make it up. In Switzerland, the difference between the Canton of Uri and the Canton of Vaud is equal to that between the fifteenth and the nineteenth centuries. Properly speaking, Switzerland has never had a federal government. The union between these two cantons exists only on the map, and their differences would soon be felt if a central authority tried to prescribe the same laws for the whole territory.

One of the circumstances that most powerfully helps to support the Federal government in America is that the States have not only similar interests, a common origin, and a common tongue, but have also reached the same stage of civilization, which almost always makes a union workable. I know of no European nation, however small, that shows less uniformity among its different provinces than the American people, who occupy a territory as large as half of Europe. The distance from Maine to Georgia is reckoned at about one thousand miles, but the difference between the civilization of Maine and that of Georgia is slighter than the difference between the habits of Normandy and those of Brittany. Maine and Georgia are at the opposite ends of a great empire, and they therefore have by nature more real inducements to form a confederation than Normandy and Brittany, which are separated only by a bridge.

The geographical position of the country added to the advantages that the American legislators drew from the manners and customs of the inhabitants, and it is mainly to this circumstance that the adoption and the maintenance of the Federal system are owed.
